At Henkels & Baker, PC, we focus our criminal defense work on exactly these charges, working with people across Dubuque and the surrounding region — including parts of Wisconsin and Illinois within roughly 100 miles of our office.

What a Felony Charge in Iowa Really Means for You

Most people don’t realize how fast things can move after an arrest. Before you even speak to a judge, key decisions get made — and without a skilled felony lawyer at your side, those decisions may not go your way. The wrong move early can close off options you didn’t know you had.

The consequences don’t stop at sentencing. A felony conviction in Iowa can strip you of your right to vote, your right to own a firearm, and your ability to work in many licensed fields. It can cost you housing, financial aid, and custody rights. These losses don’t fade with time. They stay.

At Henkels & Baker, PC, we know what’s at stake. Our team reviews your charges and the evidence right away. We look for weak points in the state’s case — improper searches, faulty evidence, and procedural errors.

Felony OWI Charges in Iowa: A first or second OWI in Iowa is considered a misdemeanor. A third or subsequent OWI within twelve years is a Class D felony under Iowa Code § 321J.2. The penalties are steep: a mandatory minimum of 30 days in jail (which the court cannot suspend) and up to five years in prison, a fine of $3,125 to $9,375 plus surcharge, and a six-year driver’s license revocation.

An OWI can also become a felony regardless of prior offenses if someone is hurt. An OWI that causes serious injury is a Class D felony, and an OWI that causes a death is charged far more seriously as vehicular homicide. As with any OWI, a felony OWI runs on two tracks at once: the criminal case in court and a separate driver’s license action through the Iowa Department of Transportation, each with its own deadlines.

Felony Drug Charges in Iowa: While simple drug possession is usually a misdemeanor, charges involving manufacturing, delivery, or possession with intent to deliver a controlled substance are felonies under Iowa Code § 124.401(1). Iowa grades these by the substance and the quantity involved, from a Class D felony up to a Class B felony, and adds further exposure for offenses near a school, park, or other protected area under Iowa Code § 124.401A.

Much of a drug case turns on what the State can actually prove — that you knowingly had control of the substance, and that the traffic stop, search, and seizure were lawful. That’s where a careful review of the evidence does the most work.

Key Facts About Felony Charges in Iowa

  • A third or subsequent OWI within 12 years is a Class D felony under Iowa Code § 321J.2.

  • A felony OWI carries a 30-day mandatory minimum and up to 5 years in prison.

  • Drug manufacturing, delivery, or possession with intent is a felony under Iowa Code § 124.401(1).

  • Felony drug charges range from a Class D felony (up to 5 years) to a Class B felony (up to 25 years).

  • A felony conviction can affect your right to vote, own a firearm, and work in licensed fields.

What to Expect When Facing a Felony Charge in Iowa

A felony case in Iowa moves through several stages. Knowing what comes next can help you feel less lost. Here is how the process typically unfolds.

  • Step 1: Initial Consultation: Your first meeting covers the basic facts. You share what happened, and we listen without judgment. This step helps us understand your situation before anything else.

  • Step 2: Case Review: We review police reports, witness statements, and any evidence related to your case. Iowa law gives you the right to see the evidence against you — we use that review to find gaps, errors, or problems with how the case was built.

  • Step 3: Building Your Defense Strategy: Every felony case is different. Some cases have strong grounds for a motion to dismiss. Others point toward negotiating a reduced charge. A few go to trial. We tell you clearly what your options are.

  • Step 4: License and DOT Track (OWI Cases): For a felony OWI, we also address the separate driver’s license action through the Iowa DOT, including deadlines to contest a revocation and the process for a temporary restricted license and ignition interlock device.

  • Step 5: Pre-Trial Hearings: In Iowa, felony cases are handled by the Dubuque County District Court. Before any trial, there are hearings covering bail, evidence disputes, and pretrial motions. We handle the court appearances and speak on your behalf at each one.

  • Step 6: Negotiation or Trial: Many felony cases in Iowa resolve before trial. The prosecutor may offer a plea deal — we explain any offer fully and honestly, and you make the final call. If a deal is not in your best interest, we prepare for trial.

  • Step 7: Sentencing or Resolution: Iowa felony sentences vary widely — from probation to prison time, depending on the class of felony and your history. We advocate for the most favorable outcome, and if the case is dismissed or results in an acquittal, we help you understand what that means going forward.

You will not navigate this alone. At every stage, you know what is happening and why.

A felony charge in Iowa can reshape your life fast. The right legal help, sought early, may improve your ability to protect what matters most.

At Henkels & Baker, PC, our team understands what is at stake when you face serious criminal charges in Dubuque. We know the local courts, the prosecutors, and how felony cases move through the Iowa system.

You Deserve Clear Answers

You deserve clear answers — not confusion — from the moment you reach out. Our tested lawyers can make a real difference in how your case unfolds, and the sooner you act, the more options you may have.

Contact us today and schedule a free initial consultation. We are here, we are listening, and we are ready to help you move forward.

1. When does an OWI become a felony in Iowa?

An OWI that causes serious injury or death is also charged as a felony, regardless of prior offenses.

  2. Which drug charges are felonies in Iowa?

    3. Simple possession is usually a misdemeanor, but manufacturing, delivery, or possession with intent to deliver a controlled substance is a felony under Iowa Code § 124.401(1). Depending on the substance and quantity, these range from a Class D felony (up to five years) to a Class B felony (up to 50 years), with added penalties for offenses near a school or other protected area.

  3. What happens if I miss my court date after being charged with a felony?

    4. A missed court date in Iowa can result in a warrant for your arrest issued the same day. Contact your lawyer right away if this happens — acting fast can help limit the damage.

  4. Will a felony charge show up before I’m convicted?

    5. Yes. An arrest record in Iowa is public, and charges can appear on background checks before any verdict is reached. This is one reason early legal help matters so much.
